text: I don't disagree with the article but it may give some readers the impression that pre-AI hand-written code wasn't fragile. Here's the famous commentary about Oracle RDBMS codebase of 25 million lines:   https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18442941  Every big company codebase with millions of lines devolves into a similar state.  The small codebase starts with clean conceptual integrity.  It then inevitably decays into incomprehensible spaghetti code as more people are added to it.  Various reasons for it including the later devs caring less about the code than the initial team of devs, deadlines, avoiding refactoring because of fear about breaking things, etc. If you don't want AI to create fragile code, you have to apply the same quality gates that would have been applied to pre-AI hand-written code to keep everything clean.  Most companies don't do that.

text: Friction is good when it serves a security purpose, not for its own sake. Too much of it and users either stop using the thing or find ways around it, which is arguably worse - as you pointed out! To have LESS friction you need MORE signals, ones that add up to "this action is low risk, proceed" as a cumulative risk score. Kind of like credit card transactions... most transactions go through silently because the issuer scores them on merchant, amount, device and history, and you only get the step-up prompt when the score is off. "Manual Approval" and "Bypass Everything" are both what you ship when you have no signals.

text: > Moore's law re-starts, because someone figures out entirely new transistor designs that can deliver at least up to 100x per-core frequency gains over Si transistors (which would be nothing considering that Si transistor tech delivered ~1Mx gains since invention) That assumes that there is no hard, physical limit on Moore's Law, which is obviously false. There is a limit, and as long as we depend on mass flow of charge through conductors, it's nowhere near quantum sizes. Where that limit is has not yet been determined, but at this point the support structure to write transistors is the size of a house trailer, using a staggering amount of toxic chemicals (just to run the exotic lasers). text: The bar for Turing-complete is very low. The halting problem is to programming as Godel's incompleteness theorem is to metamathematics. Yet no one is seriously suggesting that we downgrade to axiomatic systems incapable of expressing Peano arithmetic, nor that our current axiomatic systems are impractical for proving theorems. We cannot automatically and completely verify nontrivial semantic properties of arbitrary programs written in a Turing-complete language (Rice's theorem), but as long as we as humans can intuit correctness arguments for our programs, then formal methods will apply to it. Of course, declarative rather than imperative programming semantics tend to result in simpler correctness arguments, sidestepping reliance on global state and convoluted loop invariants.

The media coined the term  "dual quality"  for a European food scandal a few years back, in which conglomerates (including Coca-Cola) adulterated products with cheap, substitute ingredients, if they were destined for distribution in specific markets (mainly, lower-income). The packaging exteriors were the same. You wouldn't know which version you got unless you were paying close attention to taste. It was essentially what the software industry calls "A/B testing", except with sneaking things into what people eat. text: Author here. This started as a 2 m² vegetable bed and got out of hand: 8 soil probes, a weather station, a camera, and a Rain Bird valve that I control through an old Android phone tapping its own app. The part I found interesting: a fixed rules engine for watering kept being wrong in ways that needed context (forecast, last week's response, what the leaves look like). So an agent now runs every morning, reads the full history (4M readings, 62 MB in Iceberg), changes watering within hard limits, and logs what it expects to happen so it can check itself the next day. Disclosure: the data side runs on LakehouseBox, which I'm building. The code is at github.com/jatorre/garden-lake. Happy to answer anything, including "why not Home Assistant."

text: The naming of these Gemini 4 models is ridiculous. In order of sophistication and cost, the models are Hydrogen -> Argon -> Carbon. What kind of ordering is that?!? With the introduction of Hydrogen, it's no longer ordered alphabetically. That would be Argon → Carbon → Hydrogen. And it never was ordered by atomic mass, which is arguably the best ordering if you're going to name your model classes after chemical elements. That would be Hydrogen → Carbon → Argon. It's also not ordered by prevalence in the universe. That ordering would also be Hydrogen → Carbon → Argon. It's not ordered by electronegativity, boiling point, melting point, or any other remotely defensible chemical property I can think of. It's not even ordered by letter count, Scrabble score, or NFPA 704 Flammability Rating, all of which would be Argon → Carbon → Hydrogen.

text: I am copying my comment below here because there is a fundamental misunderstanding of consumer surplus here: In your example ($50/$100), the airline is extracting all consumer surplus. This is called perfect price discrimination, and it is bad for consumers. There is nothing stopping the airline offering Bob $50 per seat in the second scenario, other than profit preservation. If they were making a profit on the $50 ticket in the first scenario, they are making it in the second. They just happen to also be making less profit on the $100 ticket. In effect you are making corporate profit a constraint on the market, which is not the case. Your example actually shows that the welfare extractive pricing algos companies use today can be undermined by AI, which is good for consumers in this narrow example.

text: Railroads had some of the same issue encountered by the dotcom bubble, and in particular dark fiber: Overcapacity. Once railroads where demonstrated to be (extremely) profitable, people kept building them even if the existing demand was already met. The exact same thing happened with dark fiber (looking at you Enron). AI is a bit different in the sense that the capacity can be used for research, and more importantly is not bound to a specific connection (between locations), and therefore a lot more fungible. Not sure about canals, but while I think there are issue with current AI investments, I would not conflate them with the railroad bubble on this basis.

text: If you have a file in your repository that is not safe to run you have bigger problems than your development system getting compromised. What I mean by this is that if you restrict python execution to the entry point of your software and then Claude wants to run a command anyway so it threads it through the main.py script, you are no longer running something that is contained to your local development environment. But when you think about it, what exactly prevents Claude from doing that anyway? Claude could add malware into your project directly. So the case where you say it doesn't matter which python script it can execute, actually does matter. Restricting python execution to a subset of all files buys you security. The next step would be to get Claude to stop adding malware to your software, which it hopefully already does not do.

text: I think there's a mix of good and bad ideas in this video, but one of the things that struck me was the comment by the interviewer, Wolf Tivy, that the Linux /proc filesystem as a type of perhaps-non-deliberate vendor lock-in for the Linux operating system, since it's not like how other systems operate. But /proc is famously an idea that the Plan 9 operating system innovated, and that is in some sense a purer implementation of the Unix philosophy that everything is a file than Unix itself had - and that Linux basically appropriated wholesale because it turned out to be a useful idea. There's nothing stopping any other OS from adopting /proc, just as Linux did. It doesn't accomplish vendor lock-in at all, conceptually. And it didn't seem like either Blow or Tivy understood that.

text: It's an open source project developed in public:  https://github.com/bablr-lang  It's closest in scope to Tree-sitter, defining a parser core and the ability to run arbitrary parsers. The end goal is to replace Git and Github and tear down the structural barriers to software literacy. For example, check out our code syntax highlighter, Bedazzlr:  https://docs.bablr.org/reference/bedazzlr  Other web syntax highlighters just add colors, which paradoxically only helps you read the code if you  already  know what the code means. Bedazzlr is more like having  https://astexplorer.net/  embedded right into the blog post code snippet. You get semantic highlighting for example, and you can even see how the parser breaks things down. All in only a few KB of code! The goal is to develop it into a fully featured in-browser IDE and version control system, and to compete with Github

text: "Reason about it" is where your abstraction has sprung a leak. LLMs do what they say on the tin: they model language. If you ask an LLM "find security vulnerabilities in my code" for hello_world.rs, the next likely tokens are "I found the following vulnerabilities", regardless of what logic or reason say. It happens to be true that predicting next tokens on your own output mocks actual reasoning fairly well. But it still just a simulacrum rather than the real thing, and when held as an abstraction it leaks everywhere. Understanding this is critical to avoiding the common failure case of scope creep and code slop.
